prompt: A team adds a field in the middle of lesson 2's plain access line. What happens to the scripts that read those lines?

choices.text: They stop with a parse error on the first line they meet
choices.why: Splitting on spaces always succeeds; it just puts the wrong word in each slot.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the status stays the fourth word
choices.why: A field in the middle pushes the status to another position.

choices.text: They read the wrong column, and nothing reports it
choices.why: Right. A position is not a name; the field after the new one moves.

choices.text: The log package refuses lines longer than before
choices.why: The log package writes whatever it is given.

prompt: Why should the message of a structured line be a constant such as `"request"`, with the variable parts in fields?

choices.text: Lines with the same text are counted and grouped together
choices.why: Right. A message that differs on every line groups nothing.

choices.text: JSON cannot hold a message built with `Printf`
choices.why: It holds any string; the problem is that each one is different.

choices.text: A constant message is shorter on disk than a formatted one
choices.why: Size is not the argument the lesson makes.

choices.text: Levels only work when the message never changes
choices.why: Levels are a separate field and work with any message.

prompt: Match each idea of structured logging to what it gives an operator.

pairs.right: dropping or filtering lines by how much they matter

pairs.left: a request id carried on every line
pairs.right: finding all lines of one request together
queries such as every 5xx on one path

right_distractors: making the file smaller than plain text

prompt: In `logdemo`, the `Debug` line never appeared. Why?

choices.text: `Debug` is only printed when the program runs under `go test`
choices.why: slog does not look at how the program was started.

choices.text: The level was INFO, so DEBUG was dropped
choices.why: Right. INFO is also slog's default.

choices.text: The JSON handler has no way to write debug lines
choices.why: Any handler writes them at a low enough level.

choices.text: The line went to standard error instead
choices.why: Both handlers wrote to standard output; the line was dropped.

prompt: `logger.With("request_id", id)` returns a new logger. What does it change in what that logger writes?

choices.text: The id appears as a field on each of its lines
choices.why: Right. The field is given once and repeated on every line.

choices.text: Only its first line carries `request_id`, the rest stay as they were
choices.why: Both the error line and any later ones carry it.

choices.text: It replaces the message with the request id
choices.why: The message stays; the id is an added field.

choices.text: It changes the level of every line to ERROR
choices.why: With adds fields; the level comes from the call.

prompt: The address `ana@example.com` was logged as `a***@example.com`. What did that?

choices.text: The `email` type's `LogValue` method
choices.why: Right. slog calls it for any slog.LogValuer, so every call hides it.

choices.text: The JSON handler masks every string with an `@`
choices.why: It writes strings as they are; the type did the hiding.

choices.text: The caller wrote the masked form by hand in the log call
choices.why: The call passed `email("ana@example.com")`, the full address.

choices.text: A level that drops the local part of addresses
choices.why: Levels drop whole lines, never parts of values.

prompt: The slog handler that writes `key=value` pairs for a terminal is the ___Handler.
What does boxoffice's `requestID` middleware send back to the client?

choices.text: A cookie holding the request id
choices.why: No cookie is set; a header is.

choices.text: The whole log line of its request, in the body
choices.why: The body is the handler's answer; the log stays on the server.

choices.text: Nothing; the id lives only in the log
choices.why: The capture shows `X-Request-Id` in the response.

choices.text: The id, in an `X-Request-ID` header
choices.why: Right. A client that reports a problem quotes it.

prompt: Why must `requestID` come before `logRequests` in the chain?

choices.text: The chain refuses two middlewares that set headers
choices.why: Any number of middlewares set headers.

choices.text: The id has to be generated after the status is known
choices.why: It is made before the handler runs, so it is on every line.

choices.text: The logging middleware takes its logger from the context, filled one step earlier
choices.why: Right. Outside it, logger(ctx) falls back to the default without the id.

choices.text: Otherwise CORS rejects the request
choices.why: CORS does not look at the request id.

prompt: At which level does boxoffice's new `logRequests` write a request that answered 409?
hint: The rule is about 500 and above.

choices.text: ERROR, since 409 is a refusal
choices.why: Only 500 and above are ERROR; a refusal by the rules is INFO.

choices.text: INFO
choices.why: Right. The capture shows the 409 line at INFO.

choices.text: WARN, the level between INFO and ERROR
choices.why: The middleware uses only INFO and ERROR.

choices.text: DEBUG, so that refusals are hidden by default
choices.why: Every request is logged at INFO or above.

prompt: After `slog.SetDefault`, the `log.Printf` in `fail` comes out as JSON. What does that line still lack?
hint: Compare it with a request line.

choices.text: A timestamp
choices.why: The default handler adds `time` to every line.

choices.text: A level
choices.why: It is written at INFO.

choices.text: Fields, and the request id
choices.why: Right. The whole text is the message; converting the call to logger(ctx) adds both.

choices.text: Valid JSON: the bridge writes plain text
choices.why: The capture shows those lines as JSON objects.

prompt: Put what happens to one request in boxoffice's new chain in order.
hint: The first middleware named is the outermost.
items: `requestID` makes an id and puts a logger carrying it in the context
`logRequests` notes the start time and wraps the writer
`logRequests` writes one line with the status, size and duration

prompt: A zerolog call is written `logger.Info().Int("event_id", 1)` and nothing more. What is written?
hint: How does a zerolog line end?

choices.text: A line with only `event_id`
choices.why: Without Msg the line is never written.

choices.text: A compile error, because `Msg` is required
choices.why: It compiles; the line is silently lost.

choices.text: A line with an empty message
choices.why: Msg writes the line; without it there is none.

choices.text: Nothing: without `.Msg(...)` no line is sent
choices.why: Right. That is the classic zerolog bug, and the compiler does not catch it.

prompt: In the zerolog program, the first `Debug` line was written and the second was not. Why?

choices.text: zerolog drops repeated messages
choices.why: The messages differ, and repetition is not the rule.

choices.text: The second line had no timestamp
choices.why: Both came from the same logger with Timestamp.

choices.text: Debug lines are written once per process
choices.why: No such rule; the level changed.

choices.text: `SetGlobalLevel(InfoLevel)` was called; before it, zerolog lets everything through
choices.why: Right. slog's default drops DEBUG; zerolog's default does not.

prompt: What does zap's `SugaredLogger` give that its `Logger` does not?

choices.text: Typed fields such as `zap.Int`
choices.why: Those belong to the strict Logger.

choices.text: Lines with no allocation at all
choices.why: The sugared API allocated more bytes per line.

choices.text: Loose key-value pairs and Printf formats
choices.why: Right. Convenience, at the cost of an extra allocation.

choices.text: A text format instead of JSON
choices.why: Both wrote JSON in the capture.

prompt: Why does the zap program call `defer logger.Sync()`?

choices.text: So that buffered lines are flushed before the program exits
choices.why: Right. Without it, a crashing program loses the lines that explain the crash.

choices.text: To print the stacktrace on errors
choices.why: The production configuration does that by itself.

choices.text: To switch from the sugared API back to the strict one
choices.why: Sync has nothing to do with the two APIs.

choices.text: To wait for every goroutine that logged
choices.why: It flushes output; it does not wait for goroutines.

prompt: What does `zap.NewProduction()` add to every ERROR line, as the capture shows?

choices.text: A request id
choices.why: The program added that with With; the configuration did not.

choices.text: A colour code
choices.why: The output is plain JSON.

choices.text: The time in São Paulo's zone
choices.why: `ts` is seconds since 1970.

choices.text: A `stacktrace`
choices.why: Right. Useful once, costly on a service that logs many errors.

prompt: Match each logger to a detail of its default output in this lesson.
right_distractors: one line of text with no field names

prompt: In the benchmark, which logger wrote a line fastest?

choices.text: slog
choices.why: slog took 570 to 670 ns.

choices.text: zerolog
choices.why: Right, by a wide margin.

choices.text: zap
choices.why: zap took 450 to 470 ns.

choices.text: zap sugared
choices.why: That was the slowest of the zap APIs.

prompt: How many bytes per line did zap's strict `Logger` allocate in the benchmark?
boxoffice serves each request in milliseconds and writes one access line per request. What does the benchmark say about switching it to zerolog?
hint: Put half a microsecond next to a millisecond.

choices.text: Worth doing: zerolog is three times faster than slog
choices.why: Three times a fraction of a microsecond is invisible next to a database call.

choices.text: Worth doing, because slog allocates on every line
choices.why: slog allocated nothing per line in the capture.

choices.text: Harmful, since zerolog cannot write JSON
choices.why: zerolog wrote JSON in the capture.

choices.text: The gain is hundredths of one per cent of a request
choices.why: Right. The deciding questions are elsewhere.

prompt: Why is slog's place in the standard library the decisive row of the comparison table?
hint: Think of libraries you depend on.

choices.text: Standard library code runs faster than modules
choices.why: zerolog, a module, was the fastest.

choices.text: Modules are not allowed to write to standard output
choices.why: All three wrote to standard output.

choices.text: slog is the only one with levels
choices.why: All three have levels.

choices.text: A library accepts a `*slog.Logger` and every application passes its own
choices.why: Right. It is the shared type; zerolog or zap still sit behind it as a handler.

prompt: Which of these were measured in the benchmark? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: slog allocated nothing per line
choices.why: Right: 0 allocs.

choices.text: zap sugared allocated 384 bytes per line
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: zerolog allocated once per line
choices.why: zerolog allocated nothing.

choices.text: `LogAttrs` was slower than slog's `Info`
choices.why: It was slightly faster on both runs.

prompt: Which of these belongs in a boxoffice log line?

choices.text: The `Authorization` header, to debug staff access
choices.why: It carries a secret token; it is never logged.

choices.text: The ticket id
choices.why: Right. An id leads to the data where it is managed.

choices.text: The request body, in full, for a failed purchase
choices.why: A body holds whatever the client sent, secrets included.

choices.text: The buyer's card number, masked by hand
choices.why: Payment data stays out of the log.

prompt: Why reduce personal data at the type, with `LogValue`, rather than at each log call?

choices.text: `LogValue` encrypts the value so it can be read back later
choices.why: It returns a reduced value; nothing is encrypted.

choices.text: Every call that logs the type gets the reduced form, with nobody remembering
choices.why: Right. A rule kept by memory fails on the call that forgot.

choices.text: The law requires a method called `LogValue`
choices.why: The law speaks of personal data, not of Go methods.

choices.text: A reduced value makes the log line faster to write
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given.

prompt: Why is a log full of e-mail addresses a problem under the LGPD and the GDPR?

choices.text: Logs are not allowed to contain the `@` character
choices.why: The rule is about personal data, not about characters.

choices.text: E-mail addresses make JSON lines invalid
choices.why: An address is an ordinary string in JSON.

choices.text: It is a copy of personal data nobody finds when a deletion request arrives
choices.why: Right. The person's right to deletion reaches every copy.

choices.text: Both laws forbid logging anything about a request
choices.why: They regulate personal data; ids, statuses and durations are fine.

prompt: A service logs every 404 from clients at ERROR. What does the lesson say this costs?
hint: A log where everything is an error.

choices.text: Nothing, since a 404 is an error for the client
choices.why: The level is about the server's health, and a client's 404 is INFO.

choices.text: Real errors drown among ordinary refusals
choices.why: Right. A log where everything is an error is a log where nothing is.

choices.text: More disk, but searches stay as useful
choices.why: The searches lose their meaning, not only the disk.

choices.text: The server answers 500 instead of 404
choices.why: The level of a log line does not change the response.

prompt: An operator has the id `2e7276e971b433ac` from a client's complaint. What finds everything boxoffice wrote about it?
hint: The id is a field on the lines of that request.

choices.text: Searching the access lines for the client's address
choices.why: Addresses are not logged; the request id is.

choices.text: A search on the `request_id` field
choices.why: Right. Every line written through that request's logger carries it.

choices.text: Reading the response body the client kept
choices.why: The body holds the answer, not the server's lines.

choices.text: Restarting boxoffice at DEBUG level
choices.why: The lines already written carry the id; nothing needs to change.

prompt: Order the steps that moved boxoffice from lesson 2's lines to structured logs.
items: `requestID` gives each request an id and a logger carrying it
`logRequests` writes the access line as fields through that logger
the old `log.Printf` calls are converted one by one to `logger(ctx)`
trap: The conversion of the old calls is the remaining work, after the bridge.
